article.para: Siliko Core includes a built-in infix parser that handles traditional mathematical expressions. *Infix* refers to the fact that, in this notation, the operator is placed between the operands on which it operates, as opposed to prefix notation, such as Lisp-style S-expressions, where the operator comes first, or suffix notation, such as reverse Polish notation, where the operator comes last. The Siliko infix language also includes support for function calls, using a syntax where the function name comes first, and its arguments are passed as a comma-separated list between parentheses after the function name. The Siliko infix language supports single mathematical expression without variables or state. Whitespace characters can be used to separate tokens, but are otherwise ignored.

section.para: A number, can be either an integer, represented as a series of decimal digits, or a real, represented as a series of decimal digits, followed by a decimal point (.), optionally followed by another series of decimal digits. In a real, the decimal point may not be separated from the digit sequences with whitespace.
An integer is a series of one or more decimal digits. The tokenizer passes the series of digits to the C standard-library strtoll function to get the integer value.

A real is a series of one or more decimal digits, followed by a decimal point, optionally followed by one or more decimal digits. The tokenizer passes the series of characters to the C standard-library strtof function to get the float value.

Operators are placed between the operands on which they function. Siliko’s infix language supports six operators: `+` for addition, `-` for subtraction, `*` for multiplication, `/` for division, and `d` for die rolls. Because addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division are left associative, the infix parser builds syntax trees in reverse when parsing sequences of these operators. These operators are also implemented as functions. The infix parser automatically generates function calls from these operations.
section.literallayout: | Operations | Operators | Associativity | Function | | ------------------------ | --------- | ------------- | -------------------- | | die roll | `d` | none | `dice` | | exponentiation | `^` | right | `power` | | multiplication, division | `*`, `/` | left | `multiply`, `divide` | | addition, subtraction | `+`, `-` | left | `add`, `subtract` |
section.para: Die rolls can only take a positive integer literal as the second operand, so die rolls can’t be chained like other operands. All other operators may take arbitrairy expressions as their operands.

The Siliko infix language uses parentheses to isolate a portion of an expression from the order of operations. Anything inside a pair of parentheses will be evaluated independently of any surrounding values and operations.

Function calls take the form *function-name*`(`*arguments*...`)` `arguments` is a comma-separated list of expressions. How many parameters a function takes is defined by the function, but Siliko Core’s internal function-calling mechanism requires at least one argument for any function call.
